text: They smelled it before they saw it — woodsmoke, wrong in a way that ordinary hearth-smoke wasn't, thin and sharp and coming from somewhere that oughtn't be burning at all. Robin recognized the village before anyone said its name. It had, after all, been the first place any of this had started, though he'd have struggled to explain to a stranger how a stolen goose and a badly-aimed arrow had led, by however crooked a road, to this.
“That's—” he started.
“The geese village,” Will finished. “Small world.”
“Small county,” said Marian, already moving faster. “Which is worse.”

What they found, coming over the last rise, was not the tidy chaos of a tax seizure but something with considerably less restraint to it — a dozen men, armed and unhurried in the specific way of people who had done this before and expected no real resistance, moving through the village with torches and sacks, taking what they liked and burning what they didn't.
“Highwaymen,” said Marian, flat and certain. “Not the Sheriff's men. Worse discipline, better weapons. They've been working this road for months — I'd heard, but I hadn't heard here.”
Robin was already scanning the chaos, and found, with a lurch that had nothing to do with strategy, the small scrappy shape of a boy being dragged by the collar toward a cart that plainly wasn't his.
“That's Wat,” he said, and was moving before anyone could agree it was a good idea.

sequence._describe: The five-person crew engaging a dozen armed highwaymen in the village, Robin's arrow flying astray, Long John Little acting as a human wall, Will Scarlett-Sleeves using his sleeve as a weapon, Marian Fletcher's arrows finding their mark, more organized and dangerous opponents than previous chapters. Warm painterly storybook illustration style, expressive and slightly exaggerated proportions, rich saturated color, soft painterly brushwork, comedic tone. text: What followed had the shape of every scrape they'd survived so far — Robin's arrow going somewhere he hadn't quite intended, Long John becoming, effectively, furniture that fought back, Will's sleeve doing something no sleeve should be capable of, Marian's flawed arrows finding flaws to exploit in men who'd never troubled to check her wares — but it had, underneath the familiar chaos, a harder edge than any of it had carried before. These men did not scatter at a startled goose. They regrouped. They had, Robin realized with a cold drop in his stomach, actually been trained.
“There's too many,” Long John said, low, to no one in particular, in the tone of a man doing arithmetic he didn't like the answer to.
“There's exactly as many as there are,” said Marian, “and we deal with that number, not a smaller one we'd prefer.”

Brother Crumb, for his part, had abandoned any pretense of subtlety and was simply throwing anything within reach — a stool, a bucket, at one memorable point a live and extremely offended chicken — with the accuracy of a man who had once, apparently, thrown considerably heavier things for a living. It bought them time. It did not buy them enough.

The man leading the raiders was the one who noticed Wat first — really noticed him, the way a professional notices the thing that will make people stop fighting sensibly — and closed the distance to the boy with the flat, businesslike speed of someone who had done this calculation before and always come out ahead.
Robin got there first. It was, by any reasonable measure, the wrong decision. It was also the only one he was going to make.

text: He put himself between the blade and the boy, which worked, in the narrow sense that Wat was not struck. In every other sense, it did not work at all. Robin went down hard, a line of red spreading fast across his side, and the sound that came out of him was smaller and more frightened than anything the others had heard from him yet — not the sound of a man who'd been unlucky, but of one who'd genuinely, finally, run out.

“Robin!” Marian was there in an instant, hands pressed hard against the wound, her voice gone tight and controlled in the way of someone refusing, by main force of will, to let it become anything else.

Long John roared — an actual roar, the first anyone had heard from him — and put himself bodily between the raiders and the rest, but even he was one very large, very tired man against too many, and everyone on that hillside knew it.

“Hold him,” Marian said, to Will, to anyone, pressing harder, and there was a note in it none of them had heard from her before — not the sharp exhaustion of a woman managing chaos, but something closer to fear, carefully, deliberately not being allowed to win.
“I've got him,” Will said, and meant it, kneeling in the mud in clothes he would never, in any previous circumstance, have knelt in, one hand braced hard against Robin's side beside hers.

Brother Crumb had run out of things to throw. Long John had run out of ground to hold. For the first time since any of this had started, luck — the specific, improbable, arrow-bending luck that had carried them through geese and collectors and abbots — did not seem to be coming.

sequence._describe: An old man with a gnarled walking staff moving decisively through the chaos, a sharp-eyed boy at his heels, both unexpectedly capable and calm, the old man's staff striking down attackers with surprising precision. Warm painterly storybook illustration style, expressive and slightly exaggerated proportions, rich saturated color, soft painterly brushwork, comedic tone. text: Which was when the old man arrived.

He came down the slope at a pace that had no business belonging to a man his age, a boy — sharp-eyed, quick, unbothered by the chaos in a way that should have been alarming and somehow wasn't — at his heels. He carried no visible weapon beyond a gnarled walking staff, and he used it, in the next several seconds, to entirely rearrange the raiders' understanding of how this afternoon was going to go.

It should not have worked. An old man with a stick against trained highwaymen was not a fair fight by any measure anyone would have written down beforehand. And yet the staff found wrists and knees and the backs of legs with a precision that read, to everyone watching, as the kind of thing a very lucky old woodsman might manage on a very good day — nothing more remarkable than that, nothing anyone would think twice about once the shock wore off.

The boy, for his part, moved through the chaos like he'd been doing it his whole life, quick and low and always somehow exactly where the fight had just stopped being, and between the two of them the raiders' confidence — never especially deep to begin with — cracked, then broke entirely. The leader took one look at his scattering men, one look at the old man still advancing without any apparent hurry at all, and made the only sensible decision available to him, which was to leave, quickly, and not look back to see how undignified it was.
It was over almost before anyone still standing had time to be afraid of how it might have gone.

The old man reached them last, kneeling by Robin with an ease that belied his years, and looked at the wound with the brisk, unbothered competence of someone who had seen a great many wounds and was not especially impressed by this one.

text: “Deep, not fatal,” the old man said, already pressing a folded cloth to the wound with hands far steadier than his apparent age suggested. “You're a fortunate young man.”

“Doesn't feel it,” Robin managed, through gritted teeth, and there was something almost like a laugh in the old man's answering expression — brief, and gone before anyone could examine it too closely.
“No,” the old man agreed. “It rarely does, at the time.”

Marian, still kneeling close, looked at the old man with the particular sharp attention of a woman filing away a detail for later — the staff, the precision, the timing of it all — and said nothing, for now, though it was clear from her face that nothing was a temporary state.
“Who are you?” Long John asked, once it was clear Robin was going to survive the asking.

“An old man,” said the old man, with the mild, unhelpful cheerfulness of someone who had answered this question a great many times without ever quite answering it. “Passing through, with my grandson. We heard the trouble and came to see if we could be of use. It seems we could.”
“That's not an answer,” said Will.

“It's the only one I've got,” said the old man, not unkindly, already turning his attention back to Robin's bandaging with the air of a subject he considered closed. The boy beside him said nothing at all, but watched the five of them — Robin especially — with a quiet, careful attentiveness that none of them, in the general relief of still being alive, thought to find strange.

text: Agnes Hale found them not long after, moving through the wreckage of her village with the brisk, unbroken efficiency of a woman who had survived worse than this and intended to survive it again, Wat trailing close behind her, uncharacteristically quiet.
“You came back,” she said, to Robin, with an expression that suggested she hadn't entirely expected to have cause to say it.
“We heard there was trouble,” Robin said, wincing as he tried and failed to sit up properly.
“There's always trouble,” said Agnes, not unkindly, and then, looking at the old man and the boy with open curiosity, “And who might these two be?”

“Friends,” said Marian, before either of the strangers could answer for themselves, in a tone that made clear the word was doing a great deal of careful, deliberate work. “It seems we've made some new ones today.”

The old man said nothing to correct her. The boy, watching, said nothing at all — and if either of them looked, for just a moment, faintly relieved at how easily friends had covered the question, no one on that hillside was paying close enough attention, yet, to notice.
